title: The Meiji Restoration: How Japan Remade Itself in One Lifetime
topic: lịch sử châu Á: Duy tân Minh Trị
summary: From Perry's black ships in 1853 to the death of the Meiji emperor in 1912, how a feudal shogunate became a constitutional empire, what it cost, and why historians still argue about it.
body:
In the summer of 1853 Japan was a country of roughly thirty million people, governed for two and a half centuries by a military regime that kept foreign contact to a trickle. Fifty-nine years later, when the emperor whose reign gave the period its name died in 1912, Japan had a written constitution, an elected parliament, a conscript army that had defeated both China and Russia, a national railway network, compulsory schooling, colonies in Taiwan and Korea, and treaties with the Western powers on equal terms. Few countries have changed so much, so deliberately, in a single lifetime.

That transformation is usually called the Meiji Restoration. The name is misleading in at least two ways. It was not really a "restoration", because the emperor had not ruled in person for many centuries and the new state looked nothing like any earlier Japanese government. And it was not a single event, but a long, contested process full of civil war, assassinations, rebellions, and bitter arguments about what Japan should become. This article walks through that process: why the old order fell, what the new leaders actually did, what it cost, and why historians still argue about how to judge it.

## The world that was about to end

### The Tokugawa order

From 1603 Japan was ruled by the Tokugawa shogunate (the *bakufu*, literally "tent government"). The shogun, a hereditary military ruler based in Edo (today's Tokyo), held real power. The emperor lived in Kyoto, performed rituals, granted titles, and was treated with reverence, but did not govern.

The country was not a centralized state in the modern sense. It was divided into some 260 domains (*han*), each ruled by a lord (*daimyō*) who kept his own samurai retainers, collected his own taxes, and largely ran his own affairs. The shogunate controlled the largest share of land directly and kept the lords in line through a web of rules. The most famous was "alternate attendance" (*sankin-kōtai*): lords had to spend every other year in Edo and leave their families there as virtual hostages. The system was expensive for the lords, which was part of the point, and it turned the roads between the provinces and Edo into busy arteries of trade and culture.

Society was officially divided into status groups: samurai at the top, then peasants, artisans, and merchants. In reality the picture was more fluid. By the nineteenth century many samurai were poor salaried officials living on fixed rice stipends, while merchant houses in Osaka and Edo had grown rich. Literacy was high for a pre-industrial society, thanks to thousands of temple and private schools. Commercial agriculture, regional specialties, and credit networks had developed. Historians today stress that Tokugawa Japan left Meiji Japan a surprisingly strong base: a dense market economy, competent administrators, and a population used to the idea of orderly rule.

### The "closed country"

Foreign relations were tightly managed. After the suppression of Christianity in the early seventeenth century, the shogunate restricted contact with Europeans to Dutch traders confined to the small artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbor. Chinese merchants also traded at Nagasaki, and relations with Korea, the Ryukyu Kingdom, and the Ainu were handled through particular domains. Later writers called this policy *sakoku*, the "closed country". Recent scholarship prefers to describe it as controlled, not closed: Japan was never completely sealed off, and through the Dutch a small group of scholars studied Western medicine, astronomy, and military science, a field known as *rangaku* ("Dutch learning").

By the early nineteenth century, though, the outside world was pressing in. Russian, British, and American ships appeared more often. News of China's defeat by Britain in the Opium War (1839–1842) and the forced opening of Chinese ports alarmed Japanese officials and scholars. If the Qing empire could be humbled, what chance did Japan have?

## The black ships

### Perry's arrival

On 8 July 1853, Commodore Matthew C. Perry of the United States Navy sailed into Uraga, at the mouth of Edo Bay, with four ships, two of them steam-powered. The Japanese called them the "black ships" (*kurofune*) because of their dark hulls and the smoke from their funnels. Perry carried a letter from President Millard Fillmore asking for coaling stations, help for shipwrecked sailors, and trade. He made it clear he would return for an answer.

He came back in February 1854 with a larger squadron. Unable to resist by force, the shogunate signed the Convention of Kanagawa on 31 March 1854. It opened two ports, Shimoda and Hakodate, to American ships and allowed a US consul to reside in Japan. Similar agreements with Britain, Russia, and the Netherlands soon followed.

### The unequal treaties

The real blow came four years later. The American consul Townsend Harris negotiated the Treaty of Amity and Commerce, signed on 29 July 1858. It opened more ports to trade and residence, and it included two provisions that Japanese would resent for decades:

- **Extraterritoriality**: foreigners accused of crimes in Japan would be tried by their own consuls under their own laws, not by Japanese courts.
- **Fixed tariffs**: Japan could not set its own import duties; rates were fixed by treaty at low levels.

Britain, France, Russia, and the Netherlands quickly obtained similar terms. Together these became known as the "unequal treaties". Revising them became one of the central goals of Japanese foreign policy for the rest of the century.

The treaty also triggered a political crisis at home. The emperor Kōmei refused to approve it. The shogunate's chief minister, Ii Naosuke, signed anyway, then cracked down on his critics in what became known as the Ansei Purge, which included executions and forced retirements of prominent lords and activists. On 24 March 1860, a group of mostly former samurai from the Mito domain ambushed and killed Ii outside the Sakurada Gate of Edo Castle, in a snowstorm. The killing of the shogun's most powerful official by a band of swordsmen shocked the country and showed how weak the regime had become.

## From "expel the barbarians" to "overthrow the shogunate"

### Sonnō jōi

The 1860s were a decade of turmoil. A slogan spread among young samurai: *sonnō jōi*, "revere the emperor, expel the barbarians". It combined loyalty to the throne with hostility to foreigners and, increasingly, contempt for a shogunate that had given in to them. Foreign residents were attacked, and in 1862 samurai from the Satsuma domain killed a British merchant, Charles Richardson, on the road near Yokohama in what became known as the Namamugi Incident.

The two domains that would eventually topple the shogunate learned painful lessons. In 1863 a British squadron bombarded Kagoshima, Satsuma's capital, in retaliation for Richardson's death. In 1863 and 1864 the Chōshū domain fired on foreign ships passing through the Shimonoseki Strait and was bombarded in return by an allied fleet. Both domains drew the same conclusion: expelling the foreigners was impossible with swords and old cannon. Japan would first have to learn from them. From then on, *jōi* faded as a practical policy, while the anti-shogunate part of the slogan grew stronger.

### Satsuma and Chōshū join hands

Satsuma, in southern Kyushu, and Chōshū, at the western tip of Honshu, were large "outside" domains (*tozama*), whose ancestors had been on the losing side or neutral when the Tokugawa took power in 1600. They had long memories and, by the 1860s, modern weapons bought from Western traders. They were also rivals, and in 1864 Satsuma had helped the shogunate drive Chōshū forces out of Kyoto.

In early 1866, however, the two signed a secret alliance. The traditional story gives a starring role to Sakamoto Ryōma, a masterless samurai from Tosa who acted as go-between. Some recent historians think his role has been exaggerated in popular memory and that Satsuma officials such as Komatsu Tatewaki mattered more. Either way, the alliance changed the balance of power. When the shogunate sent a punitive army against Chōshū later in 1866, it was humiliated.

### The shogun steps down

The last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, was intelligent and reform-minded, and he tried to modernize the shogunate's army with French help. But the political tide was against him. In November 1867 he formally returned governing authority to the emperor (*Taisei Hōkan*), hoping to remain the leading figure in a new council of lords.

His opponents had other plans. On 3 January 1868, Satsuma and allied troops took control of the palace gates in Kyoto, and a proclamation announced the "restoration of imperial rule" (*ōsei fukko*). The young emperor, Mutsuhito, had come to the throne in February 1867 at the age of fourteen after his father's death. He would later be known by the name of his era: Meiji, "enlightened rule". The new regime also stripped Yoshinobu of his lands and offices. That made war almost certain.

## The Boshin War

Fighting broke out at Toba and Fushimi, just south of Kyoto, in late January 1868. The shogunate's forces outnumbered the Satsuma–Chōshū army, but the latter fought under the imperial banner, and several wavering domains switched sides. Yoshinobu fled to Edo by ship.

What followed is known as the Boshin War, after the name of the year in the traditional sixty-year calendar. In the spring of 1868 the imperial army marched on Edo. A full-scale battle for the city, then one of the largest in the world, was avoided when Saigō Takamori of Satsuma and Katsu Kaishū, the shogunate's naval commander, negotiated a peaceful surrender of Edo Castle. Yoshinobu went into retirement and lived quietly until 1913.

Resistance continued in the northeast. A coalition of northern domains fought on, and the siege of Aizu-Wakamatsu in autumn 1868 became one of the war's most tragic episodes, remembered for the young samurai of the Byakkotai ("White Tiger Force") who killed themselves believing their castle had fallen. The last holdouts, led by the shogunate's naval officer Enomoto Takeaki, sailed to Hokkaido and proclaimed a short-lived Republic of Ezo. They surrendered at the star-shaped fort of Goryōkaku in Hakodate in June 1869. Enomoto was later pardoned and served the new government as a diplomat and minister, a pattern of reconciliation that was common among former enemies.

## A new state, built from the top

### The Charter Oath

While the war was still going on, the new leaders tried to explain what they stood for. On 6 April 1868 the emperor issued the Charter Oath, a short statement of five principles. In the commonly cited English translation, it promised that "deliberative assemblies shall be widely established and all matters decided by public discussion", that "evil customs of the past shall be broken off", and that "knowledge shall be sought throughout the world so as to strengthen the foundation of imperial rule".

The oath was deliberately vague. Its authors were not committing to parliamentary democracy; "public discussion" originally meant consultation among lords and leading samurai. But the oath's language could be, and later was, quoted by people demanding much more. Its last line also became a kind of national motto for the era: Japan would borrow whatever worked, from wherever it could be found.

In September 1868 Edo was renamed Tokyo, "eastern capital", and the emperor soon moved into the former shogunal castle. In October the era name was changed to Meiji, and the government decided that from then on each emperor would have just one era name for his whole reign.

### Who actually ruled

The emperor was the symbol and source of legitimacy, but day-to-day power lay with a small group of men, most of them former samurai of middling rank from Satsuma, Chōshū, Tosa, and Hizen, joined by a few court nobles. The most important included Ōkubo Toshimichi and Saigō Takamori of Satsuma, Kido Takayoshi of Chōshū, and the court noble Iwakura Tomomi. A slightly younger generation, including Itō Hirobumi and Yamagata Aritomo of Chōshū, would dominate the later decades. Critics called this ruling circle a clique (*hanbatsu*, "domain faction"), and the charge stuck.

### Abolishing the domains

The new government's first great problem was that it still did not control most of the country. The domains had their own armies and tax systems. In 1869 the lords of Satsuma, Chōshū, Tosa, and Hizen led the way in "returning" their land registers and people to the emperor (*hanseki hōkan*), and the others followed. The lords were reappointed as governors of their former domains, so little changed in practice.

The decisive step came on 29 August 1871, when an imperial decree abolished the domains altogether and replaced them with prefectures run by governors appointed from Tokyo. At first there were over three hundred prefectures; consolidation by the end of 1871 brought the number down to about seventy-five, and after further mergers the structure that survives today (forty-three prefectures plus Tokyo, Osaka, Kyoto, and Hokkaido) was in place by 1888. The former lords were pensioned off generously and moved to Tokyo. Remarkably, this dismantling of a centuries-old system happened almost without bloodshed, partly because the government had gathered a small imperial force from the loyal domains beforehand and partly because many domains were deep in debt, which the central government took over.

## The Iwakura Mission: seeing the West

In December 1871, with the domains barely abolished, about half the senior leadership left the country. The Iwakura Mission, led by Iwakura Tomomi with Kido, Ōkubo, Itō, and Yamaguchi Naoyoshi as vice-ambassadors, sailed from Yokohama with about fifty officials and attendants and a similar number of students who would stay abroad to study. Among the students were five girls; the youngest, Tsuda Umeko, was six years old and would later found one of Japan's first private colleges for women.

The mission had two goals. The first, to begin revising the unequal treaties, failed quickly: Western governments made it clear that they would not give up extraterritoriality until Japan had legal and political institutions they considered "civilized". The second goal, to study the West, succeeded beyond expectation. Over almost two years the envoys toured the United States and Europe, visiting factories, shipyards, parliaments, schools, prisons, and museums. They noticed that the industrial gap between Japan and Britain was large but recent, measured in decades, not centuries, and that smaller states such as Prussia had built strength rapidly through state leadership. The mission's official record, compiled by Kume Kunitake, filled five volumes.

They came home in September 1873 convinced that Japan's priority had to be internal development, not foreign adventures. That conviction would soon split the government.

## Rebuilding society

The years around the Iwakura Mission saw an extraordinary burst of reforms. Some were carried out by the "caretaker government" left behind in Tokyo, some after the envoys returned. A few key examples show their scale.

### Ending the samurai class

The status system was dismantled step by step. Former samurai became *shizoku* ("gentry"), a title with little legal meaning, and commoners gained the right to take surnames, choose occupations, and marry across old status lines. In 1876 the government banned the wearing of swords in public (the *Haitōrei*) and, in the same year, converted all remaining samurai stipends into one-off government bonds. For many lower samurai, whose bonds yielded little, this meant poverty. Some became officials, teachers, police officers, or soldiers; others failed in business. The old warrior elite was abolished by its own members.

### A conscript army

In January 1873 a conscription ordinance made men liable for military service regardless of birth. The main architect, Yamagata Aritomo, had studied European armies, and the logic was both military and political: a national army loyal to the emperor would replace domain forces loyal to their lords. Many samurai were outraged that peasants would carry arms. Many peasants were unhappy too, because the draft took young men from the fields; there were riots against it in several areas. Early versions of the law also allowed various exemptions, including for heads of households and for those who paid a fee.

### A new tax

The Tokugawa regime and the domains had taxed land in rice, at rates that varied from place to place. The Land Tax Reform of 1873 replaced this with a uniform tax of 3 percent of the assessed value of land, paid in money, with landowners given title deeds. This gave the government a predictable income, which in the 1870s made up the great majority of its revenue, and created a national land market. But it shifted risk onto farmers, who now owed the same cash amount in good years and bad. Protests forced a cut to 2.5 percent in 1877. Over the following decades many small farmers fell into debt and became tenants, a social problem that lasted until the land reform after the Second World War.

### Schools for everyone

The Education Ordinance (*Gakusei*) of 1872 set out a national school system, influenced by French and American models, with the aim that "there shall be no community with an illiterate family". Building it took time, and early fees made parents reluctant. But enrollment in elementary schools rose steadily, and by the early twentieth century nearly all children attended. Universities followed, starting with what became the University of Tokyo in 1877.

### Railways, factories, and the calendar

The first railway, between Shimbashi in Tokyo and Yokohama, opened in October 1872, built with British engineering help. The Tomioka Silk Mill, a state model factory built with French expertise under the adviser Paul Brunat, was completed the same year, and silk would become Japan's most important export for decades. The telegraph spread quickly, a national postal service began in 1871, and on 1 January 1873 Japan adopted the Western solar calendar, turning the third day of the twelfth month of Meiji 5 into the first day of 1873.

### Hired foreigners

To do all this, the government employed foreign experts known as *oyatoi gaikokujin*, "hired foreigners". Estimates suggest that well over two thousand, possibly around three thousand, worked for the government during the Meiji era, and thousands more for private firms. They came from Britain (railways, navy, lighthouses), France (law, the early army), Germany (medicine, later the army and constitutional law), the United States (education, agriculture in Hokkaido), and elsewhere. They were very expensive, and the government replaced them with Japanese graduates as quickly as it could. The aim was to learn, not to depend.

## The great split

### The debate over Korea

In 1873, while the Iwakura envoys were abroad, the caretaker leaders became furious with Korea's refusal to recognize the new Meiji government in the form it demanded. Saigō Takamori proposed going to Korea himself as an envoy, expecting, some historians think, to be killed and so provide a reason for war. This debate is known as the *Seikanron*, the "debate on conquering Korea". Historians still disagree about how far Saigō wanted war and how far he sought a dramatic personal mission.

When Iwakura, Ōkubo, and Kido returned, they blocked the plan, arguing that Japan was not ready and had to strengthen itself first. Saigō resigned, followed by Itagaki Taisuke, Etō Shinpei, Gotō Shōjirō, and Soejima Taneomi. The government had split in two, and the departures shaped the next decade.

### Samurai revolts and the Satsuma Rebellion

Some of the discontented chose armed resistance. Etō Shinpei led a rising in Saga in 1874 and was executed. Smaller samurai revolts broke out in Kumamoto, Akizuki, and Hagi in 1876, provoked in part by the sword ban and stipend commutation.

The largest came in 1877. Saigō had returned to Kagoshima and opened private schools where thousands of young former samurai trained. When government agents tried to remove weapons from an arsenal there, his students rebelled, and Saigō, somewhat reluctantly by many accounts, agreed to lead them. The Satsuma Rebellion lasted about eight months. The rebels besieged Kumamoto Castle but could not take it, and the government's conscript army, backed by railways, telegraph, steamships, and money, slowly ground them down. On 24 September 1877 Saigō, wounded in the final battle at Shiroyama near Kagoshima, died there; tradition says a comrade beheaded him at his request.

The rebellion marked the end of armed samurai resistance. It also proved that an army of conscripted commoners could beat professional warriors. Saigō became a tragic popular hero; the government pardoned him posthumously in 1889, and his statue with his dog stands in Tokyo's Ueno Park. Ōkubo Toshimichi, his childhood friend turned opponent, was assassinated in Tokyo on 14 May 1878 by former samurai who blamed him for Saigō's death.

## Freedom, rights, and a constitution

### The Freedom and People's Rights Movement

Itagaki Taisuke chose a different path from Saigō. In 1874 he and others petitioned for an elected assembly, launching what became the Freedom and People's Rights Movement (*Jiyū Minken Undō*). At first it drew mainly on disaffected former samurai, but it spread to rural landowners and townspeople, who held meetings, founded newspapers, translated Rousseau and John Stuart Mill, and drafted dozens of private constitutions, some remarkably liberal. The government responded with a mix of repression, through press and assembly laws, and concession.

The decisive concession came in October 1881, after a political scandal over the planned sale of state assets in Hokkaido. An imperial edict promised a national assembly by 1890. Okuma Shigenobu, who had pushed for a quick British-style parliament, was forced out of the government, and Itō Hirobumi took charge of drafting a constitution on terms the leadership could control. Political parties formed in anticipation: Itagaki's Liberal Party (Jiyūtō) and Okuma's Constitutional Reform Party (Rikken Kaishintō).

### Money troubles and the Matsukata deflation

The new state was expensive, and the war of 1877 had been paid for partly by printing money. Inflation followed. From late 1881 the finance minister Matsukata Masayoshi imposed a harsh program: spending cuts, new taxes, and withdrawal of paper money. He founded the Bank of Japan in 1882. The policy stabilized the currency and laid foundations for later growth, but crop prices collapsed, and many indebted farmers lost their land. In 1884 debt-ridden farmers in Chichibu, near Tokyo, rose in a short armed uprising that was crushed by troops.

In the same period the government began selling many of its model factories and mines to private buyers, often on generous terms. Families and firms close to the government, such as Mitsui and Mitsubishi, benefited, and these sales helped create the large business groups later called *zaibatsu*. Supporters saw this as sensible privatization; critics saw cronyism.

### The Meiji Constitution

Itō went to Europe in 1882 to study constitutions and was most impressed by German scholars such as Rudolf von Gneist and Lorenz von Stein, who favored a strong monarch and limited parliament. In December 1885 a cabinet system was created, with Itō as Japan's first prime minister.

The Constitution of the Empire of Japan was promulgated on 11 February 1889, presented as a gift from the emperor to his subjects. Its main features:

- The emperor was "sacred and inviolable", the head of the state, and supreme commander of the army and navy.
- Ministers were responsible to the emperor, not to parliament.
- The Imperial Diet had two houses: an appointed and hereditary House of Peers and an elected House of Representatives. The Diet's consent was needed for laws and the budget, but if a budget failed, the previous year's budget could continue.
- Subjects had rights, such as freedom of speech, religion, and association, but "within the limits of law".

The first general election was held on 1 July 1890. Only men aged twenty-five or over who paid at least 15 yen a year in direct national taxes could vote, about 450,000 people, a little over 1 percent of the population. The Diet first met in November 1890. Even with these limits, opposition parties won a majority, and the Diet quickly became a real arena of conflict, especially over budgets.

In October 1890 the government also issued the Imperial Rescript on Education, which called on subjects to show filial piety, loyalty, and readiness to "offer yourselves courageously to the State" in emergencies. Copies, with the emperor's portrait, were placed in every school and read aloud at ceremonies. The rescript blended Confucian ethics and emperor-centered nationalism, and it shaped Japanese moral education until 1945.

## A modern power among empires

### Treaty revision

For the Meiji leaders, success would be measured by the West's willingness to treat Japan as an equal. In the 1880s Foreign Minister Inoue Kaoru tried to impress Western diplomats with Westernization, symbolized by the Rokumeikan, a reception hall designed by the British architect Josiah Conder and opened in 1883, where officials held balls in European dress. Many Japanese mocked it, and Inoue's draft treaty, which would have allowed foreign judges in Japanese courts, caused an outcry.

Success came through legal reform instead. With new criminal and commercial codes and the constitution in place, Japan signed a commercial treaty with Britain on 16 July 1894 that abolished extraterritoriality from 1899. Other powers followed. Full tariff autonomy came in 1911.

### Wars and colonies

The Meiji state also turned outward, and this is where its story becomes darkest and most disputed. Japan annexed the Ryukyu Kingdom as Okinawa Prefecture in 1879 and consolidated control over Hokkaido, with heavy costs to the Ryukyuan and Ainu peoples.

Rivalry with Qing China over Korea led to the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895. Japan's modern army and navy won decisively. By the Treaty of Shimonoseki in April 1895, China recognized Korean "independence", paid a large indemnity, and ceded Taiwan, the Penghu Islands, and the Liaodong Peninsula. Within days, Russia, Germany, and France forced Japan to return Liaodong in the "Triple Intervention", a humiliation that hardened Japanese nationalism, especially when Russia itself leased part of the peninsula three years later.

In January 1902 Japan signed an alliance with Britain, the first such equal alliance between a Western great power and an Asian state in the modern era. Two years later, competition with Russia over Manchuria and Korea led to the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905. Japan won costly victories at Port Arthur and Mukden and destroyed the Russian Baltic Fleet at Tsushima in May 1905. The Treaty of Portsmouth, signed in September 1905 under US mediation, gave Japan southern Sakhalin, Russia's lease in southern Manchuria, and a free hand in Korea. Many Japanese, expecting more, rioted in Tokyo over the terms.

The war's result echoed far beyond Japan. In much of Asia, including among Vietnamese patriots such as Phan Bội Châu, who launched the Đông Du ("Go East") movement to send young Vietnamese to study in Japan, it was seen as proof that an Asian nation could defeat a European empire. For Koreans, however, it meant the loss of their country. Korea became a Japanese protectorate in 1905 and was annexed in August 1910. Japanese colonial rule there, and in Taiwan, brought railways, schools, and industry, but also land seizures, political repression, and policies of forced assimilation. These remain painful and contested subjects in East Asia today.

The emperor Meiji died on 30 July 1912. General Nogi Maresuke, a hero of Port Arthur, and his wife took their own lives on the day of the funeral, an act that stunned the country and seemed to many to mark the end of an age.

## Ideas that shaped the era

### Civilization and enlightenment

The early Meiji years saw a fashion for "civilization and enlightenment" (*bunmei kaika*): Western hairstyles, clothing, beef eating, gas lamps, brick buildings. The most influential writer of the period was Fukuzawa Yukichi, founder of what became Keio University. His *An Encouragement of Learning* (*Gakumon no Susume*), published in installments from 1872, opened with a famous line usually translated as "Heaven does not create one person above or below another", and argued that independence of the individual was the basis of the independence of the nation. It sold in enormous numbers.

Fukuzawa is also associated with a 1885 newspaper editorial, *Datsu-A Ron* ("On Leaving Asia"), which argued that Japan should cut its ties with its "backward" neighbors and join the Western nations. The piece was unsigned, and scholars debate whether he wrote it, but it has come to symbolize a strand of Meiji thinking that looked down on the rest of Asia.

### "Japanese spirit, Western techniques"

Not everyone wanted wholesale Westernization. A common formula was *wakon yōsai*, "Japanese spirit, Western techniques": adopt Western science and institutions while preserving Japanese values. In the late 1880s a reaction against the Rokumeikan style set in, with writers calling for the preservation of "national essence" (*kokusui*). The government itself promoted State Shintō and emperor worship as a unifying national ideology, separating Shinto from Buddhism in 1868 in a way that led, in some places, to the destruction of Buddhist temples and images.

### The entrepreneur as patriot

On the economic side, figures such as Shibusawa Eiichi embodied the idea that business could serve the nation. Shibusawa, a farmer's son who served briefly in the shogunate and the Meiji finance ministry, founded the First National Bank in 1873 and was involved in founding roughly five hundred companies. He argued that profit-making should rest on Confucian ethics, a theme summed up in the title of his later book *The Analects and the Abacus*. Since 2024, his portrait has appeared on Japan's 10,000-yen note.

## How should we judge the Meiji Restoration?

Historians have argued about the Meiji era for more than a century, and the main positions are worth setting side by side.

### A model of modernization

One influential view, popular in Western scholarship in the 1950s and 1960s and still widely held in Japan, treats Meiji as a model of successful modernization. A non-Western country, facing colonial danger, kept its independence, built modern institutions, and industrialized within a generation. Supporters point to the leaders' pragmatism, their willingness to learn, and their careful sequencing of reforms. This reading has often been used, in Asia and Africa alike, as a lesson for later developing countries.

### A revolution, or something less?

Japanese Marxist historians before the Second World War split over the same events in what became known as the debate on Japanese capitalism. One school, the Kōza-ha, saw the Meiji state as an absolutist monarchy resting on semi-feudal landlordism, an incomplete bourgeois revolution. The other, the Rōnō-ha, saw Meiji as essentially a bourgeois revolution that had already put Japan on a capitalist path. The debate mattered politically because it shaped views on what kind of change Japan still needed. Non-Marxist historians have also asked whether Meiji was a "revolution from above", carried out by a section of the old elite against the rest of it, rather than a popular revolution.

### The road to 1945?

A third line of argument links the Meiji settlement to the militarism of the 1930s and the Pacific War. The constitution put the army and navy directly under the emperor, gave civilian ministers limited control over them, and made the emperor both sacred and politically central. The education system taught loyalty above independent judgment. Imperial expansion began in the Meiji era itself. Critics argue that these features made later catastrophe more likely.

Others push back. They point out that Japan in the 1910s and 1920s developed lively party politics, mass newspapers, and universal male suffrage (in 1925), the so-called Taishō democracy, all under the Meiji constitution. In this view, the turn to militarism had more to do with the Great Depression, the world crisis of the 1930s, and specific choices made then than with anything built into the Meiji system.

### Views from the neighbors

Finally, the Meiji era looks very different from Seoul, Taipei, Beijing, or Naha than from Tokyo. For Koreans and Chinese, its successes cannot be separated from the colonization and wars that followed. Some Taiwanese accounts of the colonial period are more mixed, weighing infrastructure and education against repression. For Ryukyuans and Ainu, the Meiji state meant the end of their own political worlds. Any fair judgment has to hold these perspectives alongside the Japanese story of national survival.

## Why it still matters

The Meiji Restoration is worth knowing for at least three reasons.

First, it shows how much deliberate institutional design can achieve when a determined elite has a clear goal and a capable society to work with. Japan did not simply copy the West; it shopped around, picking the British navy, French and then German army models, German constitutional law, and American ideas about schools and farming, and adapted them to its own needs.

Second, it shows the costs that such rapid change imposes and who bears them: samurai who lost their status, farmers squeezed by taxes and deflation, workers in early textile mills, and the peoples on Japan's periphery and in its colonies.

Third, it is a reminder that "modernization" is not a single path with a single destination. The same reforms that built schools and railways also built an emperor cult and an army that answered to no one but the throne. The Charter Oath promised to decide matters by "public discussion"; the constitution placed the most important decisions beyond public reach. Meiji Japan contained both possibilities, and the twentieth century would show which one won out, and at what price.

## Further reading

For readers who want to go deeper, good starting points in English include Marius B. Jansen's *The Making of Modern Japan*, Andrew Gordon's *A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa Times to the Present*, and Donald Keene's biography *Emperor of Japan: Meiji and His World, 1852–1912*. The nippon.com series on the Meiji Restoration offers a concise Japanese perspective online.
